action_items.item: Reproduce the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, determine which divisor is zero, and determine why errors continued after monthly-spend-feature was switched off. Fix the division and add a test covering the zero case.
Add an alert on a short-window error rate or on the ZeroDivisionError log signature, so a sharp rise pages sooner than the long-window average does.
Put the monthly-spend-feature rollout behind a staged ramp that holds or rolls back automatically when the account page error rate rises.
Reconcile the flag provider's change timestamps with the evaluation logs, and record in the incident's evidence which source gives the true time the flag was enabled.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} while broken (baseline {errors_before}) and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The sustained-error alert paged at {alert_raised}, which was {alert_raised - began} after the onset.
The failing requests were logged as ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, starting at the onset. Account pages had been logged as rendering normally before it.

The spend-summary path was being reached because monthly-spend-feature evaluated on for a growing share of requests from the onset. The flag provider's change record shows the flag switched on by an admin, but that entry is stamped after the onset, so the record does not line up exactly with the log evaluations.

Switching the flag off did not help. The service stayed at the incident's level until the action was judged refuted, and the flag was then put back. So the flag state alone does not explain why the errors continued.

Nothing was deployed in the day before the incident, which rules out a code release as the trigger. The only production changes read were the flag toggles. The evidence stops here: it does not show which value is zero at spend_summary.py:47, or why the errors persisted with the flag off.

contributing_factors.factor: The sustained-error alert evaluates an average over a long window, so paging came well after the onset ({alert_raised - began}). The flag was therefore reverted only after that delay had passed.
The flag went from partial to full exposure within a minute of the onset. No check was seen that gated the rollout on error rate, and no test of the spend-summary path with a zero divisor was seen.

The flag change record is stamped after the errors began, while the evaluation logs show the flag on from the onset. This made it harder to tell whether the flag was the trigger, and the revert did not resolve it.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers using io-shop saw account pages fail. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} while the service was broken, against {errors_before} beforehand, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service was still not back to normal when the incident was closed, so it was broken for at least {duration}. These figures are lower bounds. Argus found the errors came from a spend-summary feature flag that had been enabled and switched it off. The service stayed at the incident's level, so Argus judged that action refuted, put the flag back as it had been and escalated to people. The cause was not confirmed and the service was not seen recovering.

went_well: Argus read every available channel and acted on the flag candidate within seconds of the investigation starting.
Argus restored the flag to its prior state once the revert was refuted, so its own change was not left in place.
Argus escalated to people when no explanation held.
went_wrong: The leading candidate was refuted, and the service stayed at the incident's level while Argus waited for the verdict on the revert.
The incident closed with the cause unconfirmed and the service not seen recovering.
The flag change record and the logs disagree on when the flag was enabled, which weakened the trigger attribution.

input.root_cause: Account page requests failed with a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 in the spend-summary code path, which was being exercised from the onset as monthly-spend-feature evaluated on. The evidence does not show why the division fails, and it does not show why errors continued after the flag was switched off, so the underlying cause is not established.
